items.title: [Fast Company] GM just did 34,000 years of battery testing in less than a month. Here’s how
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Developing new EV battery technology takes years of research. General Motors, for example, says it’s put a decade of effort into lithium manganese-rich, or LMR, batteries, which aren’t yet in any of their vehicles on the road.

But recently, the automaker says it made a big leap in that work. Using computer modeling, GM was able to virtually test more than 300,000 LMR battery pack configurations, advancing from first concept to formal approval in under a month. 

That represents more than 300 million CPU hours, which would take a typical computer 34,000 years, while running 24 hours a day, to complete, according to GM.

GM is leaning into artificial intelligence and virtual simulations to develop its vehicles. That not only speeds up the time to do testing, per the company, but allows it to test more options, rather than picking the best of just a few configurations. 

Those 300,000 formulations, for example, looked at different chemical combinations, temperature cycling, and other approaches to creating a battery cell, Sterling Anderson, GM’s chief product officer, told Fast Company. 

“If we had not had the luxury of some of these tools, we would have had to sample more sparsely from what was possible,” he says. 

Speeding up vehicle development

GM is bringing this AI approach beyond battery testing and into all areas of its vehicle development, with the aim of slashing the time it takes to develop a car in half. 

Typically, cars are developed within a four- or five-year time frame. That allows a “limited number” of all kinds of tests, Anderson says, from wind tunnel to crash tests. 

“Now in the virtual world, instead of the X crash test that we could have done, or Y prototypes that could go through, we can run X times 100 and Y times 1000,” he says. 

GM is also working to advance its autonomous driving capabilities with real-world and virtual testing. Hundreds of data-collection vehicles are currently driving across the country collecting 1 million miles of data a month, while virtually, GM systems drive more than 3 billion simulated miles a day.

By cutting vehicle development down to about two years, GM also says it can adapt more quickly to external challenges. Many car makers were counting on Biden-era EV tax credits to help their sales, for example, but then the Trump administration cut those credits. 

Tariffs, the war in Iran’s effect on gas prices, changing regulations, and uneasy consumer sentiments have all added uncertainty to automakers’ future product lineups, which may have been in development for years. 

A shorter development cycle “makes you more agile,” Anderson says. 

LMR batteries in the works

GM wants to be the first automaker to deploy LMR batteries, and Anderson says they’re on track to make that happen. 

LMR batteries can have 33% more energy density than lithium iron phosphate chemistry, and use a higher amount of less-expensive minerals (like manganese) rather than more of the most expensive minerals like cobalt and nickel. That allows them to offer more range—potentially more than 400 miles—at a lower cost and lighter weight. 

GM is also preparing to roll out its fourth-generation EV platform, which includes not only LMR batteries but a centralized, upgraded computing system, and new electrical work. 

It will have 30% less wiring than GM’s current EVs and 40% fewer parts in its motors and power electronics, which make it lighter and more efficient. 

GM and LG Energy Solution are working on these batteries as part of a joint venture called Ultium Cells. They plan to start commercial production of the LMR battery cells in the U.S. by 2028, at the Ultium Cells facility in Spring Hill, Tennessee.

items.title: [downes.ca] Principles and Practice of Deep Representation Learning
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Sam Buchanan, Druv Pai, Peng Wang, Yi Ma, GitHub, Oct 22, 2026

This is "a modern fully open-source textbook exploring why and how deep neural networks learn compact and information-dense representations of high-dimensional real-world data." It's a daunting read - and to be honest, I gave the first chapter a careful read but have only skimmed the rest (though it's now on my virtual bookshelf for future reference). I think people who are serious about understanding how we learn and how machines emulate this should at the very least read that first chapter. It contains what is to my understanding an accurate history of artificial intelligence (including the important early work in computation, cybernetics, and information theory). The aim of the book is to give us a framework that explains how neural networks work to generate intelligence. They authors write, "intelligence is not about collecting all informative data in advance and training a model to memorize their (low-dimensional) distribution. Instead, it requires computational mechanisms that can continuously improve current knowledge of the distribution and acquire new information when needed. A fundamental characteristic of any intelligent being or system - whether an animal, a human, a civilization, or the entire scientific community - is the ability to continuously improve or gain new information or knowledge on its own."

items.title: [scitechdaily.com] Stanford team revives bleached corals through brief clone contact
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Stanford researchers report that bleached coral fragments fully recovered within seven weeks in laboratory tests after brief contact with healthy, genetically identical clones, according to a study published Oct. 14 in *Science Advances*. Contact lasting five days to a week was sometimes enough; bleached fragments kept a few millimeters away from healthy partners died. Microscopic channels in the corals’ tissues aligned, allowing beneficial algae to move between fragments within three days. Inside bleached fragments, algae populations doubled every four days during the second week. The method requires matching clones, limiting its use across reefs. The researchers plan to test other ways to deliver algae, including collecting it from healthy corals before heat waves.

After 21 hours, the marsh surface had eroded by an average of just 7 millimeters, while its vegetation suffered progressive damage. Their effect declines as waves grow higher and vegetation is lost. Researchers say marshes could work alongside dikes and seawalls, not replace them. A Spanish coastal-engineering expert questioned how well the Dutch experiment applies to other coastlines, citing wave periods and mobile seabeds among other factors.

items.title: [Fast Company] AI fear is driving employees to slack off, show up late, and even steal coworkers’ lunches
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

As more businesses adopt artificial intelligence, some employees—who are increasingly worried about losing their jobs—are starting to act out.

That’s the finding of a new study from Washington State University researchers, published in the journal Occupational Health Science, that looks at how AI adoption at work is affecting workers’ attitudes and behaviors in the office.

Research has shown that the increase of AI-based technologies at work—such as intelligent robotics, automated systems, and algorithmic management—may make employees feel insecure about their jobs and lead to more stress and less engagement.

Washington State University’s study looked at employees across 18 different industries and found that workers who had the greatest fears about being replaced by AI were more likely to behave poorly by, for example, slacking off at the office or even stealing a coworker’s lunch.

Researchers also found that employees who assumed they would be displaced were more likely to “morally disengage” at work, such as by coming in late for a shift or surfing the web while on the clock.

“Moral disengagement is basically a way of justifying bad behavior,” Tahira M. Probst, a professor of psychology at WSU Vancouver and lead author of the study, said in a news release. “We know what’s right and wrong. We know what organizational policies say we can and can’t do. Moral disengagement is a way of reframing that behavior as something that is acceptable.”

Researchers used the AI Industry Exposure index to identify which industries were most exposed to potential AI disruption. Workers in finance and insurance had some of the highest levels of exposure, while workers in agriculture, forestry, and construction had the least. Not surprisingly, the bad behavior was more pronounced in the industries with the highest amount of disruption.

The study’s bottom line: When employees feel their jobs are at risk, they may look at workplace expectations differently and rationalize behaviors such as cutting corners or undermining coworkers to protect themselves or compensate for what they perceive as injustice.

The findings also suggest that AI anxieties can hurt workers and businesses alike, pointing to the need for employers to be more mindful of how they roll out AI in the workplace so employees are better supported.

items.title: [Fast Company] Healthcare has a churn problem
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

I was diagnosed with anorexia at 10 years old. Over the next several years, my family and I navigated a healthcare system that was mostly focused on how many days I stayed in a hospital bed instead of whether I was getting better.

I spent my entire freshman year of high school in and out of facilities, counting down 45-minute therapy slots while fighting a brain disorder that forces you to battle your own mind upwards of six times a day. The bills came in, claims were processed, and the checkboxes were ticked, but I was still struggling with anorexia.

Decades later, now as a founder and CEO of an eating disorder treatment program, I realize my teenage experience embodied the traditional healthcare business model to a T.

THE ONLY INDUSTRY WHERE PRODUCT FAILURE IS PROFITABLE

In traditional healthcare, revenue is tied to volume: More time in session results in more revenue. The more appointments booked, the more the facility can bill; the longer someone stays in treatment—and the more times they relapse—the more profitable the facility becomes.

If any consumer tech or hardware startup ran on this model, it would fail fast. It’s like going to an auto repair shop that charges by the hour, sends you home with a car that still stalls, and then charges you again when you have to tow it back into the shop.

The main problem is industry alignment. Fee-for-service models reward visit volume and usually lead to fragmented, episodic care. Value-based outcome models, on the other hand, tie reimbursement directly to clinical and financial outcomes. If we want a healthcare system that can keep up with rising costs and demand, we need to align incentives around real, measurable outcomes.

BUILD WHAT WORKS

Tying financial compensation to real-world outcomes gives leaders the flexibility to build better products that result in positive outcomes for all parties involved. In healthcare, that means patients, their families, providers, and health insurance plans.

For example, when we started Equip, we knew that once-a-week therapy wasn’t enough to address a complex eating disorder, but the traditional fee-for-service billing system made it nearly impossible to bill for anything else. By partnering with forward-thinking health insurance plans to develop value-based payment structures, we designed the treatment model families needed: a team of doctors, dietitians, therapists, and coaches delivered virtually. This approach provides the right dose of care when patients need it, without uprooting their daily routines or stopping them from building a life worth living.

WHAT DOES “GOOD” LOOK LIKE?

The catch, however, is that the healthcare industry has historically lacked a consensus on what “good” means. Defining quality is particularly difficult in eating disorders, where recovery isn’t as simple as a blood test or a healed bone. The field uses two tools—the EDE-Q and the PARDI-AR—to set severity thresholds, but neither gets into what “getting better” means. It also requires a long-term view, which can clash with an industry where most health insurance plans operate on 12- to 24-month budget cycles.

When I was 10, that meant staying in a hospital bed long enough for my vitals to stabilize. But as I found out through many cycles of treatment, that didn’t lead to me getting better.

To solve the national mental health crisis, we need an economic framework where doing good and doing good business are the same. By replacing the traditional model with outcome-based partnerships, we aren’t just building more efficient companies, but delivering on healthcare’s biggest promise: building a product that works.

Kristina Saffran is cofounder and CEO of Equip.

items.title: [library.hbs.edu] AI agents spread as job, safety and investment risks draw scrutiny
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Companies and governments are adopting AI agents that can carry out tasks, while researchers and policymakers examine their effects on jobs, security and investment. Google CEO Sundar Pichai said he uses agents to summarize internal discussions and track computing use, but humans still make consequential decisions about allocating resources. Google has also introduced agentic AI for public agencies, and the United Arab Emirates plans to shift half of federal government operations and services to autonomous agents within two years. Stanford University researchers report that employment in AI-exposed software development and customer-service jobs fell by more than 4% this year, while Harvard researchers say current labor-market signals offer little certainty about AI’s longer-term effects. Central bankers are assessing potential effects on wages and productivity, and a University of Hawaiʻi analysis estimates that AI investment and related stock gains have supported U.S. growth and consumer spending. Security teams report difficulty verifying agents’ answers, and AI infrastructure borrowers, including CoreWeave, face rising credit risks. Center for Internet Security senior director of threat intelligence TJ Sayers said autonomous AI attacks are no longer hypothetical. Agent use remained in single digits across almost every business function, according to the Stanford 2026 AI Index cited by The National.

items.title: [fortune.com] AI models uncover decades-old PHP flaws, heightening cyberattack risks
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Researchers at cybersecurity firm Calif used OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model to find a critical flaw in PHP. Google-owned security company Wiz independently used Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI models to identify vulnerabilities in the same core software. PHP maintainers released fixes on Oct. 21 for the two flaws, which had remained hidden for years and could let attackers run code on vulnerable servers without authentication. Wiz said frontier models made a complex exploit chain substantially easier to execute, describing steps that had once been at the edge of what human researchers could achieve. The same capabilities could help attackers adapt exploits to different PHP versions and server configurations, the company warned. OpenAI said it believes researchers found the flaws before attackers did. It is proposing a repeatable process for identifying and fixing vulnerabilities in widely used software and preparing defenses against them. The company said it expects similar discoveries to increase sharply in coming months.
